intent: Isolate archive signing and publishing from application training (ADR 0013 stage B)
Validate isolated training output before publication

name: Isolated archive publisher
role: Rechecks the store under the lease and publishes an archive using metadata derived from the output file
conditions: The caller provides the intended workload manifest and prevents other writers during publication

subject: Archive signatures authenticate the publisher
why: A signature does not establish that application-generated archive bytes are safe

title: Derive archive metadata in the publisher
why: The publisher computes size and digest for the output file and uses the intended workload description supplied by its caller
alternative: Trust a manifest written by the training step — rejected: its metadata may not describe the output

intent: Define separate training and publisher pod identities

name: Isolated trainer pods
role: Separate application execution from archive signing and publication using distinct pod identities
conditions: The training identity and node metadata access must not grant archive publication privileges

subject: A signature does not validate archive behavior
why: The application and JDK may influence the bytes that the trusted publisher signs

title: Use separate pod identities for training and publication
why: Cloud workload identities attach to pods, so separate identities let clusters restrict training credentials independently from publishing
alternative: Use separate containers in one pod — rejected: cloud identity can remain reachable from the training container

intent: Copy training output into publisher-owned storage

name: Publisher private archive copy
role: Copies the training output into temporary publisher-only storage before deriving metadata and uploading
conditions: The publisher's temporary directory must not be mounted into the training pod

subject: A copied archive can still contain malicious JVM data
why: A private copy stabilizes bytes between hashing and upload but does not attest the producer's behavior

title: Stabilize archive bytes in publisher-owned storage
why: The private bounded copy makes the bytes hashed by the publisher the same bytes supplied to the upload
alternative: Hash and upload directly from the shared handoff volume — rejected: another writer could change the file between those operations

name: Isolated publication command
role: Builds an intended workload fingerprint and invokes the isolated publisher with registry and signing access
conditions: The publisher process must start in a sanitized environment and use a trusted JVM and application layout

subject: Target JVM options are data
why: Setting them as the publisher JVM's own startup options could execute an application-controlled agent before the command runs

title: Pass target JVM options as separate data
why: Target options contribute to the archive fingerprint without needing to be applied to the trusted publisher JVM
alternative: Inherit application JVM startup options in the publisher — rejected: an agent option could execute application code with signing credentials

intent: Create and monitor an isolated training pod

name: Isolated training pod runner
role: Creates a named training pod, waits for completion, and requests cleanup with a UID precondition
conditions: The caller constructs the pod and the cluster must restrict the training identity and cloud credentials

subject: A create response can be lost
why: An ambiguous create failure may leave a pod even when the coordinator never received its UID

title: Delete training pods using their created UID
why: The UID precondition prevents cleanup from deleting a different pod that reused the same name
alternative: Delete the pod by name alone — rejected: a replacement pod could be removed after a race

intent: Create a per-run shared volume handoff

name: Per-run handoff directory
role: Provides a unique group-writable shared-volume subdirectory for one training run
conditions: The claim supports POSIX group ownership and only the stopped training pod has written the handoff before cleanup

subject: Handoff cleanup can encounter untrusted files
why: Cleanup avoids following symbolic links and bounds traversal so training cannot redirect it outside the run directory

title: Use a unique shared-volume directory per run
why: A fresh directory separates one run's archive from stale outputs and can be mounted as a subPath for the training pod
alternative: Reuse a fixed handoff directory — rejected: a failed run could leave output that a later publisher mistakes for its own

name: Isolated training coordinator
role: Checks the store, coordinates a training pod and invokes publication with a per-run handoff
conditions: Publication must recheck the store while holding its lease; a non-successful or unknown training result retains the handoff

subject: Pod deletion is asynchronous and creation can have an ambiguous outcome
why: Removing the handoff while a training pod may still be running can race its writes

title: Retain handoffs when training state is uncertain
why: A timeout or lost API response can leave a training pod running, so the coordinator cannot safely assume the shared directory is no longer in use
alternative: Always delete the handoff after requesting pod deletion — rejected: Kubernetes deletion can be asynchronous and race active writers

name: Training pod factory
role: Builds a training pod with a dedicated service account and a per-run handoff mount
conditions: Operator configuration and cluster admission must keep the training identity and its cloud metadata credentials unprivileged

subject: Pod specs can carry credentials through more than volume mounts
why: Secret references in environment entries and projected volumes also need validation

title: Validate training pod credential paths before creation
why: The training pod must not receive the publisher's signing or push Secret through its configured environment or volumes
alternative: Copy the application pod spec without inspection — rejected: it could carry publisher Secrets, projected tokens or host access

intent: Start the publisher JVM with a restricted environment

name: Isolated JVM launcher
role: Starts an explicitly configured trusted Java executable with only coordinator and publisher environment variables
conditions: The launcher and Java executable must come from a trusted publisher image; cluster configuration must not supply application-controlled executable paths

subject: JVM startup options are consumed before Java application code starts
why: A javaagent or dynamic loader setting could execute untrusted code before Java code can sanitize its own environment

title: Filter publisher environment before starting Java
why: An explicit allowlist removes application-controlled JVM and loader options before the trusted publisher JVM starts
alternative: Remove unsafe options inside the Java command — rejected: the JVM may already have loaded an agent before the command runs

name: Training handoff manifest validation
role: Checks the training manifest against the independently described workload and the privately copied archive
conditions: The training manifest is untrusted and compatibility checks do not establish that its producer or archive is benign

subject: A matching fingerprint alone does not cover all JVM archive requirements
why: Archive use also depends on classpath file times and launch location

title: Reject handoffs that report a different runtime or archive
why: Comparing the training report and private archive copy against the publisher's workload description catches accidental image, JDK and output drift before signing
alternative: Ignore the training manifest entirely — rejected: ordinary mismatches could be signed and only surface when pods try to use the archive

name: Isolated coordinator command
role: Builds a workload fingerprint, runs a separate training pod and publishes a checked handoff under a lease
conditions: The publisher must use a trusted JDK, a sanitized launcher environment, a distinct service account and a shared claim whose group matches the training pod

subject: A projected service-account token describes the coordinator identity
why: The coordinator compares its token subject with the training service account; Kubernetes authenticates the token during API requests

title: Refuse a shared training and coordinator service account
why: Separate service accounts let Kubernetes and the cloud provider enforce different permissions for training and publishing
alternative: Allow both pods to use the same service account — rejected: that can grant the training pod the publisher's cloud identity
